newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Crime costs Australia A$18 billion a year, report.
newsitem.headline: Crime costs Australia A$18 billion a year, report.

text.p: Crime in Australia is costing the country at least A$18 billion (US$13 billion) every year, or more than four percent of gross domestic product, according to an Australian Institute of Criminology report.
The report said crime was costing each Australian about A$1,000, or A$2,800 for each household, adding "the largest components of these costs are the result of white-collar crime".
Australian Attorney-General Daryl Williams said on Thursday the report provided a catalyst for crime prevention strategies.
"The economic cost...is only one of the damaging effects of crime on our society, but provides a tangible example of the extent to which crime does touch us all," Williams said in a statement.

Heading the list of crime costs was fraud and forgery, which cost Australia up to A$3.5 billion every year, while drug offences (not including drug-related theft and property crime) cost at least A$2.0 billion and shoplifting cost A$2.46 billion.
The report said drug offence costs arose mainly from the treatment of drug-related illness, accidents resulting from drug abuse, premature death and law enforcement.
Police, justice system and prison costs were included in the total A$18 billion spent on crime each year.
The report found that the least common crime, murder, was also the most the expensive with about A$1.0 million spent on each homicide case.

This amount did not include prosecution, trial or jail costs, but did take into account the costs of supporting surviving dependants of both the victim and offender as well as income lost by the imprisoned offender, the report said.
